I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, things planned long ago, in complete faithfulness and tru', it moves through themes of holiness, judgment and calls readers toward hope.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows holiness lived out in assyrian crisis, exile hope. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh, you are my God. I will exalt you! I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, things planned long ago, in complete faithfulness and truth.
He will destroy in this mountain the surface of the covering that covers all peoples, and the veil that is spread over all nations.
He has brought the high fortress of your walls down, laid low, and brought to the ground, even to the dust.

questions.question: What is happening in Isaiah 25?
questions.answer: In 12 verses, this chapter isaiah 25 (12 verses) continues the story of holiness. starting with 'yahweh, you are my god. i will exalt you! i will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, things planned long ago, in complete faithfulness and tru', it moves through themes of holiness, judgment and calls readers toward hope. The setting is assyrian crisis, exile hope, written to judah. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Isaiah and why 25 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally isaiah son of amoz, addressed to judah around ~700 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as prophecy — its themes of holiness, judgment build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'faith' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Trust, loyalty to God. In this chapter, it appears in context of holiness. For a first-time reader: think of it as trust, loyalty to god, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through holiness and judgment, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 4 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'For you have been a stronghold to the poor, a stronghold to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shade from the heat, when the blast of the dreaded ones is like a ...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about holiness. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
